title: Can a Daughter Still Claim Her Inheritance If Brothers Mutate Property in Their Own Names?
question: Can a daughter claim her share of inherited property if her brothers got it transferred only in their own names through a mutation?
body:
In many Pakistani families, land inherited from a father is quietly transferred into the names of sons alone through a "mutation" in the revenue record, often leaving daughters unaware that they have been cut out. Pakistani courts have repeatedly dealt with such disputes, and their decisions offer useful guidance on whether a daughter can still recover her share even after such transfers.

## What Pakistani courts have held

**Dr. Aziz Ur Rehman and others V. Noor Bibi and others, CLC 2021 106 (Balochistan High Court)** dealt with a daughter who sued her brothers and others, arguing that mutations and a claimed gift in the brothers' favour were illegal and that the property had later been sold to third parties without her consent. The trial court and appellate court both ruled in her favour, finding the alleged gift never proven, since mere transfer of possession does not make a gift valid. The High Court upheld this, holding that a legal heir's right to inherit does not expire with time because limitation does not apply to void transactions, that co-sharers cannot transfer more property than their own share, and that buyers from such co-sharers can only get rights in the sellers' share, not in the rightful heir's portion.

**Bibi Shah Gul v. Saadia, CLC 2010 1440 (Balochistan High Court)** involved a daughter, Saadia, who sued relatives after they allegedly mutated her late father's property into their own names, excluding her. Courts confirmed she was a legal heir entitled to half share, and a will favouring another relative was found forged. This finding was upheld all the way to the Supreme Court. When execution of the decree began, another heir objected to how the property was divided. The High Court dismissed her objections, holding that disputes about executing a decree must be resolved by the executing court itself, not through a fresh lawsuit, and that having failed to object earlier despite knowledge of the proceedings, her claim had no merit.

**Mst. Sehat Bibi V. Bahar Khan and 2 others, CLC 2018 299 (Balochistan High Court)** concerned a sister and brother who were the only surviving children of their father. The sister sued after discovering that her brother had mutated their father's land into his own name and then sold it, claiming the land had been gifted or willed to him. Lower courts had ruled against her, but the High Court overturned these decisions, finding the brother failed to prove any gift or will, produced no witnesses, and the mutation document did not even bear the father's signature. It held that both siblings were entitled to their proportionate shares and one heir cannot claim sole ownership through an unproven gift, ordering the brother to pay the sister her rightful share from the sale proceeds.

**Rashida V. Ghous-Ud-Din and 8 others, CLC 2016 533 (Balochistan High Court)** involved a woman whose attorney allegedly executed a "gift deed" transferring her inheritance share to her brother during ongoing litigation, without her knowledge. The High Court ruled in her favour, holding that a valid Islamic gift requires a clear offer, acceptance, and actual delivery of possession—none of which existed here. It also found her power of attorney did not specifically authorise gifting away her property, so the gift deed was fake and the resulting decree legally worthless. The court set aside the decree and ordered the property distributed among all legal heirs according to Islamic inheritance shares.

**Ghous-Ud-Din V. Rashida and 3 others, YLR 2014 293 (Balochistan High Court)** concerned two daughters who sued for their inheritance shares after their father's death, while other family members claimed the daughters had already gifted away their shares informally. There was no written document proving this, only oral testimony. Trial and appellate courts ruled in favour of the daughters, and the High Court upheld this, also noting that new construction built by the defendants on the disputed property created no additional rights for them since it was built without the co-heirs' permission.

## Points to keep in mind

- Courts have held that a mutation transferring property only into brothers' names does not by itself defeat a daughter's inheritance share, especially where no valid gift or will is proven.
- Courts have held that claims of gift or will require solid evidence—written documents, proper witnesses, and proof of offer, acceptance, and delivery of possession—mere oral claims or unsigned mutation entries are not enough.
- Courts have held that limitation does not apply to void transactions, meaning a daughter's right to inherit does not necessarily expire simply because time has passed since the mutation.
- Courts have held that co-sharers cannot transfer more than their own share, so anyone buying from them only acquires rights in that share, not in the excluded heir's portion.
- Courts have held that once a decree recognising an heir's share becomes final, disputes about how it is executed must generally be raised before the executing court itself, and delay in raising objections can weaken a claim.

title: Murder Convictions in Land Disputes: Can Appeals Courts Overturn or Reduce Them?
question: Can a murder conviction be overturned or reduced on appeal when the killing arose from a property or land dispute between families?
body:
In Pakistan, many murders arise from bitter disputes between families over land or property, and these cases often end up before the High Courts on appeal. The case summaries below show that appellate courts can uphold, overturn, or send back such convictions depending on the quality of the evidence and the fairness of the trial, not simply on how serious the crime appears.

## What Pakistani courts have held

**Noor Zaman V. The State (YLR 2018 1702, Balochistan High Court):** A man was convicted and sentenced to death for shooting his brother dead after a property dispute. The High Court upheld the conviction and death sentence, holding that eyewitness testimony from family members present at the scene should not be discarded merely because of their relationship to the victim, especially when it is consistent and supported by medical evidence. The court also held that a weak motive does not weaken a case built on solid eyewitness evidence, and that a long trial or time spent on death row is not by itself a reason to reduce a death sentence.

**Abdul Samad and 3 others V. The State (YLR 2018 2053, Balochistan High Court):** Four men convicted of murdering a man during a property dispute between families were acquitted on appeal. The High Court found serious contradictions among the eyewitnesses, including disagreement over weapons used, the number of vehicles involved, and the timing of the incident, as well as it being suspicious that none of the closely related eyewitnesses were injured despite an attack by eight armed men. Applying the principle that doubt must benefit the accused as a matter of right, the court set aside the convictions and life sentences.

**Abdul Manan and another V. The State (MLD 2020 1477, Balochistan High Court):** Two men convicted of murder after a dispute were acquitted on appeal. The High Court noted that it was suspicious the accused themselves took the injured man to hospital rather than the complainant who claimed to be present, that an important witness questioned by police on the first day was never produced, that another witness's statement was recorded five days late without explanation, that no fingerprint tests were conducted, and that there was no prior enmity to explain a motive. The court held that these unexplained gaps created reasonable doubt, entitling the accused to acquittal as of right.

**Abdul Hadi v. the State (YLR 2012 687, Balochistan High Court):** A man convicted of murder following a property dispute between relatives had his conviction and life sentence upheld on appeal, even though he had not personally fired the fatal shot. The High Court relied on consistent testimony from two independent witnesses matching the victim's dying declaration, and held that common intention to kill could be inferred from the accused's conduct — arriving with an armed companion, threatening the victim, and helping the shooter escape — making him equally liable under the principle of shared common intention.

**Muhammad Bakhsh v. the State (YLR 2011 2768, Balochistan High Court):** Four men convicted of murder arising from a family dispute over agricultural land had their convictions set aside because witness statements had been recorded without being read back to the witnesses as required, which the court held caused real prejudice and amounted to a miscarriage of justice. One accused, against whom no eyewitness gave direct evidence, was acquitted outright, while the case against the remaining three was sent back for a fresh, properly conducted trial. The court stressed that judges must actively safeguard fairness in criminal trials, particularly in serious cases.

## Points to keep in mind

- Courts have held that a murder conviction arising from a property or land dispute can be upheld, reduced, or overturned entirely, depending on the strength and consistency of the evidence rather than the nature of the underlying dispute.
- Courts have held that eyewitness testimony from family members is not automatically unreliable, but contradictions between eyewitnesses on key details, such as weapons, timing, or escape routes, can create reasonable doubt sufficient for acquittal.
- Courts have held that gaps in investigation, such as withheld witnesses, unexplained delays in recording statements, or missing forensic tests like fingerprinting, can undermine the prosecution's case even in a serious murder charge.
- Courts have held that procedural lapses during trial, such as failing to read back witness statements as required by law, can amount to a miscarriage of justice warranting a fresh trial.
- Courts have held that a person who does not personally inflict the fatal injury can still be held equally liable for murder if their conduct shows a shared common intention with the person who did.

title: What Happens When a Bank Sues a Borrower and Guarantors Over an Unpaid Loan
question: What happens when a bank sues a borrower and guarantors in court for failing to repay a loan?
body:
When someone in Pakistan takes a loan from a bank and fails to repay it, the bank can go to a special Banking Court to recover the money from both the borrower and any guarantors who backed the loan. Several court decisions show how these cases actually play out - including what happens if a person isn't properly notified, misses a deadline, or challenges how the bank calculated what is owed. This article looks at what Pakistani courts have said in such disputes.

## What Pakistani courts have held

**Messrs Noor Flour Mills v Judge Banking Court, CLD 2011 1263 (Balochistan High Court):** A bank sued a flour mill and its guarantor for loan recovery. When the defendants asked for permission to defend the case and submitted supporting documents and objections, the Banking Court dismissed their request without properly examining any of it, and ruled in the bank's favor. The High Court held that even in fast-track banking recovery cases, a court must issue a "speaking judgment" - one that clearly addresses the arguments and documents put forward by each side. Because the Banking Court's order failed to do this, the High Court set it aside and sent the case back for a proper decision.

**Muhammad Ali v Branch Manager National Bank of Pakistan, CLD 2011 982 (Balochistan High Court):** Here, a bank sued a borrower and two guarantors for over Rs.12.9 million. When the defendants did not respond to notices sent by post, courier, and newspaper publication, the Banking Court decided the case without them (ex parte) and ruled for the bank. One guarantor only learned of the decree when he was arrested during recovery proceedings, and he later claimed he was never properly served and that the loan documents were fraudulent. The High Court rejected his appeal, holding that service through newspaper publication was valid under the law, that he had avoided earlier attempts at service, and that he offered no good reason for waiting 21 days after his arrest to challenge the decree.

**Muhammad Musa and 2 others v National Bank of Pakistan, CLD 2024 751 (Balochistan High Court):** In this case, a bank sued a borrower over an unpaid agricultural loan of about Rs.1.4 million, and when he did not appear, the Banking Court proceeded against him and decreed the suit. On appeal, the borrower argued he was never actually served with notice. The High Court examined the record and found the bailiff's and courier's reports were missing or silent on whether service had truly been completed. Since the law requires courts to properly verify service - through bailiff delivery, registered post, courier, or newspaper publication - before proceeding against an absent defendant, the court held the borrower had been "condemned unheard" and sent the case back for a fresh trial with a chance to defend himself.

**Messrs Sabir Traders and another v National Bank of Pakistan, CLD 2023 247 (Balochistan High Court):** In this dispute, a bank recovered over Rs.73 lakh from borrowers through the Banking Court, and the borrowers appealed, claiming they were never properly heard. However, the High Court found their appeal itself was filed 12 days after the 30-day deadline set by the special law governing bank recovery cases. The court held that the general law allowing delays to be excused did not apply, because banking recovery cases follow their own strict, independent timeline. The borrowers also failed to give the bank required advance notice of their appeal. As a result, the appeal was dismissed without the court even examining its underlying merits.

**Bank of Khyber v Nazamuddin (case summary, no citation provided):** The Bank of Khyber sued a borrower to recover money owed under an Islamic financing facility. Both sides agreed to have a Chartered Accountant examine the accounts, whose report showed both principal and mark-up outstanding. The borrower objected that the bank had charged mark-up on top of previous mark-up each time the facility was renewed - effectively compounding it like interest. The court agreed this was improper, since compounding mark-up would turn an Islamic facility into a conventional interest-bearing loan. Facing this, the bank's own lawyer dropped the claim for mark-up and asked for only the principal amount.

## Points to keep in mind

- Courts have held that banking courts must issue reasoned, detailed judgments addressing the specific arguments and documents raised by defendants, even in fast-track recovery cases.
- Courts have held that proper service of notice - whether by post, courier, or newspaper publication - is essential before a case can proceed without a defendant, and that missing or unclear service records can require a case to be retried.
- Courts have held that defendants who evade or avoid receiving court notices cannot later use lack of service as an excuse to escape a decree.
- Courts have held that special banking recovery laws set their own strict deadlines for appeals, which are not softened by the more flexible general limitation rules.
- Courts have held that compounding mark-up upon mark-up in Islamic financing facilities is improper, as it can turn such a facility into an interest-based loan.
